s0.p1: Human milk is the gold standard for infant feeding. Infant formula development has moved from matching human milk in nutrition, to matching its structure, and now towards matching its flavor. Infant formula is already close to human milk in macronutrients but still differs clearly in flavor, which affects how well infants accept it and may also shape their later food preferences. Identifying the key flavor compounds of human milk, and how formula differs, is the first step towards matching its flavor.
s0.p2: This page takes one human milk sample as an example of the complete analysis. Sample HM_Test is one of the 50 human milk samples of Cui et al. (2026, Food Bioscience, doi:10.1016/j.fbio.2026.110162), and its volatile profile is close to the average of the 50 (ranked 2nd, 3rd and 2nd for closeness to the mean by three distance measures). Steps 1 to 8 use only this sample and published data; step 9 uses the mean data of the author group for 303 human milk samples and 20 infant formula samples. Each step gives the question, the tool (the links load the same input), the result, the interpretation and the limitations.
s1.q: Question: Which target compounds are in the GC-MS peak table of one human milk sample, and in what proportions?
s1.tool: Tool: GC-MS flavor interpreter, example 4 (the original instrument report of HM_Test, an Agilent MassHunter library search with 345 peak records). The standard file holds the 75 compounds and retention times of Table S1 of Cui et al. (2026); retention time range ± 0.3 min, relative content normalized to the targets, author group threshold values.
s1.r1: 27 target compounds were found (normalized over these 27). Octanoic, hexanoic and decanoic acid and hexanal have the highest relative contents.
s1.i1: Interpretation: compared with the data processing program developed by the author (same peak table). The author's program finds 29 of its 125 target compounds and normalizes over these 29; this tool finds 27 of the 75 Table S1 compounds (1-decanol and 3-heptenoic acid are not in Table S1) and normalizes over these 27, so each value is about 1.002 times the author's. Normalized over the same 27 compounds, the two agree for all of them, with a largest difference of 0.005 percentage points. The retention times in Table S1 are 0.1 to 0.3 min earlier than those measured for HM_Test, hence a range of ± 0.3 min; ± 0.2 min misses 4 compounds such as nonanal and (E)-2-nonenal, and ± 0.1 min finds only 16.
s1.lim: Limitations: Relative contents are semi-quantitative (no internal standard). The tool does not re-identify peaks and takes the library search results as they are; a wider retention time range is more likely to take in misidentified peaks (none here). 2,4-Di-tert-butylphenol, 2-ethyl-1-hexanol, 2-phenoxyethanol and isophorone are migrants from sampling containers and laboratory materials (Table S1, footnote A); they stay in the standard file, but none was detected in HM_Test.
s2.q: Question: Which compounds contribute most to the aroma of HM_Test?
s2.tool: Tool: The “flavor interpretation” step of the same page, which computes the relative odor activity value (ROAV); example 4 selects the author group values automatically.
s2.fig: The ranking table in the tool (top 10): thresholds in mg/kg; odor descriptions from the flavor knowledge base or the model.
s2.alt: Screenshot of the ROAV ranking table of GC-MS example 4
s2.i1: Interpretation: 9 key flavor compounds have ROAV ≥ 1 (eight aldehydes, one ketone), led by (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal (ROAV 100) and 1-hepten-3-one (83.4). Hexanal has the highest content of these 9 (13.1%) but a higher threshold, so its ROAV ranks only 6th. The ROAV uses odor detection thresholds in water from the compilation of van Gemert (2011) (author group values).
s2.lim: Limitations: ROAV shows only the relative contributions within one sample, not whether a compound can be smelled; the thresholds are for water, not for the milk matrix.
s3.m.66-25-1: fatty 3rd; grassy 9th; the model has no “tallow”
s3.m.3913-81-3: the model has no “tallow”: no comparison
s3.q: Question: Does the predicted odor agree with the odor descriptions in the literature?
s3.tool: Tool: Odor prediction (a graph neural network giving probabilities for 138 odor descriptors). Each compound in the table links to its prediction; the literature descriptors are those of Flavornet (Acree & Arn, flavornet.org).
s3.i1: Interpretation: 8 of the 9 compounds have at least one Flavornet descriptor among the top 5 predictions, including the metallic note of 1-hepten-3-one (4th). The exception is (E)-2-decenal: Flavornet gives only “tallow”, which is not one of the model's 138 descriptors. Descriptors outside the top 5: cucumber ((E)-2-nonenal, 10th), waxy ((E,E)-2,4-nonadienal, 12th), grassy (hexanal, 9th), green (nonanal, 6th), soapy and lemon (octanal, 11th and 23rd) and nutty ((E)-2-octenal, 29th); “fried” and “tallow” are not model descriptors. Ranks are counted over all 138 descriptors.
s3.lim: Limitations: All 9 are common compounds and all are in the model's dataset (the odor prediction page says so): 7 in the training split, (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal and octanal in the test split, so the agreement here says nothing about predictions for new molecules. Flavornet compiles odorants detected by GC-O in the literature and their descriptors; these are not the sniffing results of this study. The model does not distinguish cis/trans isomers: (E,Z)- and (E,E)-2,4-decadienal get the same prediction.
s4.q: Question: Does the estimate from gas-phase thresholds rank the compounds as the FD from AEDA does?
s4.tool: Tool: Gas-phase intensity curves, with the dose-response curves and gas-phase thresholds of Wakayama et al. (2019). The relative content in HM_Test divided by the gas-phase threshold is set against the FD of the pooled sample of 50 human milks in Cui et al. (2026).
s4.i1: Interpretation: hexanal and octanal have high ratios (both FD 64), nonanal and heptanal low ratios (FD 4 and 1): the two rankings agree.
s4.lim: Limitations: Only these 4 aldehydes have intensity curves; (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal, 1-hepten-3-one, (E)-2-nonenal, (E)-2-octenal and the other key flavor compounds have no curve in Wakayama et al. (2019) and cannot be checked.
s5.q: Question: Which molecules smell like 1-hepten-3-one (2nd by ROAV)? In which foods has it been found?
s5.tool: Tool: Ingredient and substitute search, mode B (similar molecules by cosine similarity of the predicted odor), and the compounds detected in human milk and its key flavor compounds in the flavor knowledge base.
s5.r1: The closest molecules to 1-hepten-3-one are (Z)-1,5-octadien-3-one (0.978) and 1-octen-3-one (0.977); 1-octen-3-one is also a key flavor compound identified by Cui et al. (2026) (FD 64, metallic). The predicted odors of the aldehydes are very similar to each other (for example nonanal and octanal 0.995): the model puts them in one fatty, citrus-like aldehydic group, so substituting one for another means little.
s5.r2: The knowledge base grew with the research: at first the knowledge base held only FlavorDB2 data: 1-hepten-3-one had no food source at all, “Milk Human” was linked to only 3 molecules, and none of the key flavor compounds of human milk was included. Adding FooDB did not change this, because its human milk entries are nutrients such as fatty acids, amino acids and vitamins. So the author added the published human milk data to the knowledge base (see update log 7.5); the human milk page now holds the compounds detected by Cui et al. (2026) and 10 key flavor compounds.
s5.warn: No flavorings in infant formula: GB 2760-2024 Table B.1, the list of foods to which flavorings may not be added, includes 13.01 infant and young child formulas. Its footnote a allows vanillin, ethyl vanillin and vanilla bean extract in follow-on and young child formulas, at most 5 mg/100 mL, 5 mg/100 mL and as needed for production, and states that no flavoring at all may be added to formulas whose scope covers infants aged 0 to 6 months. Infant formula therefore cannot be improved by adding key flavor compounds directly; improvement can only start from precursors (fatty acid composition, lipid sources); see steps 7 to 9.
s5.lim: Limitations: Mode B compares predicted odor only and does not show whether the molecules can replace one another; FlavorDB2 records presence only, with no amounts.
s6.q: Question: Where do the molecules detected in human milk lie on the odor map?
s6.tool: Tool: Odor map with human milk and cow milk overlaid (over 5,000 molecules arranged by predicted odor).
s6.fig: Human milk (blue; large dots: the 10 key flavor compounds) and cow milk (red) on the odor map; grey: other molecules.
s6.alt: Odor map screenshot: positions of human milk and cow milk molecules
s6.r1: The knowledge base links 100 molecules to human milk, 99 of which are on the odor map (thiamine is not in the map's molecule library): 78 come from Cui et al. (2026), 29 from FooDB (10 from both) and 2 only from FlavorDB2. These 99 molecules lie mainly in the fatty and green regions (top predicted descriptor fatty for 22, green for 20, together 42%); the 207 molecules of cow milk are more spread out (odorless 29, fruity 28, fatty 22, green 16, phenolic 12, fishy 11, sulfurous 9; fatty and green together only 18%).
s6.i1: Interpretation: this distribution is consistent with the view that human milk aroma is dominated by aldehydes and ketones from lipid oxidation.
s6.lim: Limitations: The two data sources are not comparable: the human milk data come from the author's published research, the cow milk data from FlavorDB2 and FooDB, so this does not show that cow milk lacks these compounds (many are hidden bulk entries, or the public databases have not recorded them).
s7.q: Question: If improvement starts from precursors, what do linoleic acid and α-linolenic acid taste like themselves? These two were chosen because the random forest importance ranking of Cui et al. (2026) puts them first among the precursors of human milk flavor (normalized scores 1.00 and 0.83, clearly above all other precursors).
s7.tool: Tool: Taste prediction (a graph neural network for sweet, bitter, umami and tasteless; judgement thresholds sweet 58%, bitter 42%, umami 18%, chosen on the validation split).
s7.i1: Interpretation: both linoleic and α-linolenic acid are predicted bitter, above the judgement threshold. But both are in the training data (labelled bitter), so this only shows that the model reproduces the dataset record, and that record agrees with the literature: Stephan et al. (2000) found free linoleic and linolenic acid to have the lowest bitter thresholds in emulsions and to be the main source of the bitterness of soybean lecithin; Gläser et al. (2021) found free α-linolenic and linoleic acid to be key bitter compounds in pea protein; the bitter compounds identified by Huseynli et al. (2025) in sunflower press cake include α-linolenic, linoleic, oleic, palmitic and stearic acid; Cheon et al. (2021) report that C18 free fatty acids are mainly described as bitter. Eicosanoic acid, not in the training data, is also predicted bitter (56%), in the same direction as the conclusion of Cheon et al. (2021), but a single example cannot prove the model's ability.
s7.i2: Note that in infant formula the fatty acids are added as triglycerides (oils). Mattes (2009) points out that triglycerides themselves are not effective taste stimuli; free fatty acids are. The model's prediction for triglycerides is an extrapolation and is not used here.
s7.h3: Supplement: free amino acids of human milk
s7.aa1: Human milk protein is mainly intact protein, then peptides; free amino acids are a small share but may be among the main contributors to taste. Agostoni et al. (2000) and Chuang et al. (2005) both report far higher free amino acid contents in human milk than in formula. The table lists the 17 free amino acids of the 50 human milk samples in Table 2 of Cui et al. (2026); glutamic acid is the most abundant (704 μmol/L, 49.2% of the 17 together).
s7.aa2: Interpretation: the predictions broadly agree with common knowledge: glutamic and aspartic acid umami; serine, glycine, threonine and alanine sweet; leucine, isoleucine and phenylalanine bitter. All these amino acids are in the training data, so this only shows that the tool works within its domain. Threonine (umami 34%) and cystine (umami 31%) exceed the umami threshold although the dataset does not record them as umami: a bias of the model itself.
s7.lim: Limitations: The model ignores concentration, matrix and synergy, and most molecules in the tables are in its training data. It cannot be used for safety assessment.
s8.ala.gb: ≥ 12 mg/100 kJ (≥ 50 mg/100 kcal), no upper limit
s8.dha.gb: optional (Table 4): 3.6 to 9.6 mg/100 kJ; if DHA is added, at least as much ARA, ARA ≤ 19.1 mg/100 kJ
s8.q: Question: Can 1-hepten-3-one be used as a flavoring? What do the rules say about the precursors?
s8.tool: Tool: Regulatory lookup (1-hepten-3-one, with 1-octen-3-one as a control).
s8.r1: Searching the texts of GB 2760-2024 Tables B.2 and B.3 (China), the EU Union list (consolidated version of 2026-02-16) and US 21 CFR Parts 172, 182, 184 and 189 with the FDA list “Substances Added to Food” under every spelling of the name and the CAS number (2918-13-0) finds no 1-hepten-3-one (as of the site's data date); GB 2760 has only its isomer 4-hepten-3-one (S1262). So even leaving Table B.1 aside, it is not on the flavoring lists of any of the three. As a control, the same search finds 1-octen-3-one in China (S0219), the EU and the FDA list (FEMA 2677), so the search works.
s8.r2: Infant formula may not be flavored (GB 2760-2024 Table B.1, see step 5); the precursors are governed by the nutrient standards:
s8.r3: GB 10765-2021 also requires a linoleic to α-linolenic acid ratio of 5:1 to 15:1.
s8.lim: Limitations: The site's regulatory lookup covers only the flavoring lists, not nutrient standards; the latest official texts prevail.
s9.q: Question: Where does the flavor of infant formula differ from human milk, and in which direction should it be improved?
s9.tool: Tool: The “my GC-MS data” mode of the dairy flavor improver; one click loads human milk vs CMF or human milk vs POF. The input is the mean relative content of each sample group from the author group, arranged in the tool's CSV format (download: human milk HM (n=303, target), cow-milk-based formula CMF (n=10), plant-oil-based formula POF (n=10)); human milk is the target and each formula type in turn the current sample; thresholds are the author group values (given in the CSVs), identical to the group's thresholds for its 27 key flavor compounds. These data were measured with the same instrument (Agilent 8890B) and the same fibre (DVB/CAR/PDMS) as the data of Cui et al. (2026).
s9.h3a: Human milk ROAV: tool and author group values side by side
s9.r1: The author group computes ROAV for each sample and then averages; the tool computes it from the mean contents, so the values differ (the tool fixes the largest at 100) and only the ranks are compared. The main compounds rank the same: the top 6 ((E,E)-2,4-nonadienal, 1-octen-3-one, 1-hepten-3-one, hexanal, (E)-2-nonenal, nonanal) and ranks 11 to 13 are identical. The exceptions are two swapped neighbouring pairs: (E)-2-octenal and octanal (ranks 7 and 8), and (E)-2-decenal and (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal (ranks 9 and 10). The tool finds 3 more compounds with ROAV ≥ 1 than the author group: (E,E)-2,4-decadienal and 2,3-octanedione (both below 1 in the group's values) and 1-octen-3-ol (not listed in the group's human milk results).
s9.h3b: Gaps between formula and human milk
s9.fig: Odor profiles of cow-milk-based formula (solid) and human milk (dashed), human milk / formula 12-dimension view.
s9.alt: Radar chart screenshot of CMF against human milk in the dairy flavor improver
s9.r2: Cow-milk-based formula (CMF): 18 compounds compared (values are differences in contribution share, in percentage points). Higher in human milk: (E)-2-nonenal +10.0 (not detected in CMF), 1-octen-3-one +7.0, 1-hepten-3-one +5.4, hexanal +3.6, (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal +2.5; higher in CMF: dimethyl trisulfide −9.8 (not detected in human milk), dimethyl disulfide −6.4 (not detected in human milk), (E,E)-2,4-decadienal −5.6, 2-heptanone −5.3 (not detected in human milk), pentanal −3.9, (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal −3.3.
s9.r3: Plant-oil-based formula (POF): 20 compounds compared (values are differences in contribution share, in percentage points). Higher in human milk: (E)-2-nonenal +10.0 (not detected in POF), 1-hepten-3-one +5.8, 1-octen-3-one +5.7, (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal +4.7, (E,Z)-2,4-decadienal +2.7; higher in POF: pentanal −7.0, dimethyl trisulfide −6.7 (not detected in human milk), 2-heptanone −5.1 (not detected in human milk), dimethyl disulfide −3.8 (not detected in human milk), (E,E)-2,4-decadienal −2.3.
s9.i1: Interpretation: both formula types differ from human milk in a similar direction: (E)-2-nonenal, 1-hepten-3-one, 1-octen-3-one and (E,E)-2,4-nonadienal contribute more in human milk. This agrees with the author group's conclusion: the flavor compounds of human milk are dominated by unsaturated aldehydes and ketones, and 1-hepten-3-one and 1-octen-3-one are often described as metallic (1-octen-3-one: mushroom, metal). Dimethyl disulfide and dimethyl trisulfide are higher in formula; the group links them to onion- and garlic-like notes, typically formed by Strecker degradation of methionine. For compounds higher in human milk the tool gives directions only, no amounts, and notes that infant formula may not be flavored, so only raw materials, processing and precursors can change; compounds higher in formula have to be lowered through raw materials or processing (for example oxidation control, heat treatment and storage).
s9.i2: Lipid sources (author group data): all 10 CMF contain raw cow's milk; OPO structured lipid (1,3-dioleoyl-2-palmitoyl glycerol) appears in 6 CMF and 5 POF; the lipid sources of POF include no raw cow's milk or cream and are mainly OPO and vegetable oils (soybean, sunflower, coconut, rapeseed, palm and others), 2 of them with added DHA. The author group notes that CMF and POF differ in aroma because their composition differs.
s9.lim: Limitations: The input is the mean of each group, which loses the variation between samples, and each formula group has only 10 samples; ROAV is semi-quantitative, so the two sides are compared by contribution shares, not by value; this step gives directions only, no amounts.
s10.l1.l: semi-quantitative; relies on library identification; reference retention times offset
s10.l2.l: ROAV is relative within a sample; thresholds are for water
s10.l3.l: compounds are in the dataset; no cis/trans distinction
s10.l5.l: predicted odor only; infant formula may not be flavored
s10.l6.l: human milk and cow milk data are not comparable
s10.l7.l: ignores concentration and matrix; most molecules in the training data
s10.l8.l: the lookup covers flavoring lists only
s10.l9.l: inputs are means; directions only, no amounts
s10.p1: This case starts from one raw instrument report and uses 7 tools in turn: data processing (results match the author's program) → selecting the key flavor compounds (ROAV) → checking against literature odor descriptions and FD → finding that flavorings are not allowed, which turns the work to precursors → checking the taste and the nutrient rules of the precursors → finding the gaps and the direction of improvement from the means of 303 human milk samples and 20 infant formula samples. Each tool on its own answers one small question; only together do they lead from a peak table to a direction of improvement.

s10.d7: Odor descriptors: Flavornet (Acree & Arn, flavornet.org).

case.full: A complete flavor analysis with this site's tools
case.sub: Starting from the original GC-MS report of one human milk sample, the site's 7 online tools are used in turn to find the flavor gaps between infant formula and human milk.
